items_missed: Never asked 'how are you today?' or any warm-up. The call went from 'How can I help you?' to 'did you booked it online fully?' to 'What is the email address that you use?' in four exchanges.

No agenda statement and no 'sound good?'. She opened with 'before we get too far in, are there any like, concerns or just important questions that you have top of mind that I can just kind of dive into first' — which is a good customer-first move and earns the moving-stressor bullet — but it is the opposite of a roadmap. The customer had to guess at the structure and said so: 'cause we'll cover on this call like what a little bit more details about the move and then, okay.' Twenty-eight minutes later he still had not been told what the call would cover or how long it would run.

Additional rooms never asked at the origin. No garage, no storage unit, no balcony or patio probe on a downtown high-rise where a storage cage in the garage is standard. She asked about the patio only at the destination, and only as an access question ('are we going through like the patio').

Packing needs never asked. The customer said 'fifteen ish fifteen to twenty' boxes and she confirmed that was standard, but nobody asked whether he wants them packed. On a customer with a corporate-downtown schedule moving on a Thursday morning, that is a live service question that was never put.

The entire pricing section was skipped — 4/20, and 4 of those points are automatic N/A grants on the trip fee and packing pricing. No hourly rate, no per-mover framing, no what's-included list, no disassembly/reassembly mention, no 'pricing is super simple,' no 'no hidden fees' pitch. This matters more than it would on a normal already-booked consultation because she raised the reserved time by two and a half hours on this call and never once said what an hour costs. The customer's only reaction to a materially bigger bill was 'Yeah, I'm hoping it doesn't take that long cause I don't have too much staff' — he was reacting to hours, not dollars, because dollars were never mentioned.

No Worries Damage Coverage never mentioned. The customer is moving a heavy full-length mirror he specifically called out as 'a heavy mirror so it's not like a, you know one that goes on the back of the door kind of thing. It's a piece of furniture' — down a freight elevator, through a parking garage, sixty feet to a truck. That is the exact item and the exact route that generates a damage claim, and he never heard that the move carries $2,000 of coverage.

On-Time Guarantee never mentioned — and the arrival window was actively discussed and then corrected on this call ('we'll arrive between 8:30 and nine we'll actually be arriving between 8:00 and 830 actually'), on a downtown Thursday where the customer himself raised rush hour. There is no better setup in this week's sample and it went unused.

2.5 hour minimum never stated, and the fifteen-minute proration never stated. The only clock mechanic that landed was the start trigger, and it landed sideways as an aside about parking: 'it may take us fifteen minutes to just park but the time doesn't start until we like get to you.' The customer accepted a 6.5-hour reservation without knowing how partial hours bill.
No typical time range for a one-bedroom was ever stated. She moved the number from four hours to six and a half without an anchor the customer could evaluate it against.

Crew size never stated. The truck was named ('a 26 foot box truck') because the customer asked for it, but how many movers are showing up was never said on a call that just reserved six and a half hours of their time.

Drive time never mentioned. This is 1601 Elm Street in downtown Dallas to Frisco Square — roughly thirty miles and, leaving mid-morning, a real chunk of the billable clock. The word 'drive' does not appear in the call. That omission alone could be a meaningful share of the 2.5 hours she added.

Save Your Ass speech almost entirely absent — 1/10. The only trace is 'if you're ready to go and they're just wrapping and padding that furniture and getting it all down to that truck. Then I mean things will run smooth,' which gestures at readiness but never names the mechanism. No 'prep before move day means a shorter move and a lower bill,' no consolidation examples, no carload tip, no 'does that make sense?' close.

No 'reply with any corrections' on the updated confirmation email. She said 'I am gonna send you an updated, an updated confirmation email. Okay, just so you have that I do have all the updated notes in the system as well and so that way we're just kind of all on the same page and there's no surprises' — the intent is exactly right and the ask is missing. On a call whose entire value was capturing a confusing two-address dock route ('1552 Patterson Street... the entrance to the delivery bay is on the corner of Patterson Street And Bolton Street... it's called Bolton Street truck terminal or city of Dallas dock'), asking him to read it back and correct it is the highest-value fifteen seconds available and it was not spent.
BOLDED key details at the top of the email never mentioned.
Hours and how to reach us never given. 'just let us know' and 'just give us a shout' were used four times with no number and no hours.
Customer's name used once — 'We're gonna work this out though. We're gonna get you Bobby' — short of the 3+ standard, on a twenty-eight minute call.

Efficiency: twenty-eight minutes on a one-bedroom with fifteen to twenty boxes, and no pricing delivered. The first-location parking question was worked three separate times ('where would the truck be parking', then 'if they don't fit underneath there for whatever reason, where would that', then again after the dock address) before it was written down.
top_strength: The access discovery on this call is the best in the week's sample by a wide margin, and it is the reason the move will not blow up on 9/24. The customer opened with a warning — 'the address that you have to go to, to get to my building, currently isn't the same address as the building' — and Chauny did not let it go until she had a complete, branching operational plan. She got the dock address ('1552 Patterson Street... 75201'), confirmed the cross street and the terminal name, established truck fit from the customer's own precedent ('I took a U-Haul down there when I initially moved in and it fit'), and then, critically, built the fallback before anyone needed it: 'let's just say, if they don't sit underneath there for whatever reason, where would that, what does that parking look like?' She read the whole thing back for confirmation — 'what I put here is the movers will be going into the ground. If the truck doesn't fit underground, then we'll have to park on the backside of the building. Is that, is that accurate?' — and then told him exactly how the crew would receive it: 'I got both scenarios in the move alert section for the movers, like, here's option one. If this happens, okay, this is the address that we're gonna attempt first. If this doesn't work out then we're gonna park over here.' She also measured every leg of the walk in school buses (sixty feet garage-to-elevator, one bus on the twentieth floor, twenty to thirty feet at Frisco), caught the freight elevator reservation on her own recall — 'oh, I didn't ask will you be able to reserve that freight elevator at the first location?' — and raised the rush-hour risk unprompted. Second strength, and it is not a small one: she volunteered local knowledge that built real trust. 'now I know the Frisco square very well, so let's just see what part of the building you're on' produced an exchange about the circle drive and where the Amazon trucks park that the customer completed himself ('It's off of John Elliot drive' → 'Yup, mm-hmm correct'). That is a customer who now believes the crew knows where they're going. Third, she was honest about the estimate change rather than burying it: 'now originally the system had you fitted for about three to four hours we're gonna need to increase that for sure' — delivered up front, with the reason attached, which is the right instinct.
coaching_note: Highest-leverage fix, and it is a sequencing problem rather than a skill problem: Chauny spent twenty-eight minutes doing genuinely excellent operational discovery and then delivered zero of Einstein's value story. Pricing scored 4/20 and all four points were automatic. The customer left this call not knowing the hourly rate, that there is a 2.5 hour minimum, that the clock prorates in fifteen-minute increments, that the move carries $2,000 of No Worries Damage Coverage, that he will get an email with his mover's photo, or that a late arrival starts discounting his bill. On an already-booked consultation it is tempting to treat all of that as covered by the online flow — it is not. He booked through a form; nobody has ever said any of it to him. The fix is a ninety-second block at the end of every consultation call: 'Before I let you go, quick reminder of how this works — $XXX per hour per mover, that covers the truck, gas, taxes, insurance, all the pads and wrap and the tools for disassembly, and there are no hidden fees of any kind. Two and a half hour minimum, then we prorate in fifteen-minute chunks so you're not paying for a full hour you didn't use. Your move carries No Worries Damage Coverage, up to $2,000 to repair, replace or reimburse. You'll get an email a few days out with a photo of your actual mover. And if we miss that 8:00 to 8:30 window, we start discounting immediately. Does that all make sense?' That block is worth roughly fourteen points of this score and it costs ninety seconds of a twenty-eight minute call. Estimate-accuracy flag for the bottom-4 review — this is the one Amanda should pull the actual on. Chauny raised the reservation from four hours to six and a half on a one-bedroom with a love seat, a full bed, fifteen to twenty boxes, and a customer who twice said he does not have much stuff. That is a 62% increase over the system estimate. Some increase is clearly right — the B3-to-20th-floor freight elevator with a sixty-foot garage haul is real. But listen to the reason she gave: 'we definitely just wanna make sure we have this truck reserved for like a, a decent amount of time so that they're not having to the rush because we have a move after this.' That is padding for the dispatch schedule, not for the job, and it is the cleanest example of the conservative-padding pattern in this week's batch because she said the quiet part out loud. The second reason she gave — 'we really don't know about the first location just yet like if we're gonna fit' — is uncertainty, and uncertainty is exactly what the customer was about to resolve for her: he said 'I'll have to call and like go further down and ask my leasing office like, if the truck will fit... And then I can call you guys back and update it.' The right move was to hold the four-hour reservation, tell him to call back with the dock answer, and adjust once. Instead the number moved first and the information came second. Also worth noting: thirty miles of Dallas-to-Frisco drive time never entered the conversation at all, which means part of that 2.5 hour cushion may be covering something she could have quantified. Second priority: close the loop on the email. She captured a two-address dock route, a cross street, a terminal name, a contingency parking plan and four walk distances — and then sent it without asking him to check it. 'Bobby, I'm sending that updated confirmation over now — give it a quick read and reply if I got any of that dock address wrong, because that's the piece I want to be dead certain on.' Third, the Save Your Ass speech is a 1/10 on a call that is practically designed for it: a sixty-foot garage haul, a shared freight elevator, twenty boxes, and a customer who said 'I'm hoping it doesn't take that long.' 'Here's how you get that number back down, Bobby — anything you can take down to your car in the week before, take it. The closet odds and ends, the loose stuff in drawers, the small TV, the rugs. Every trip you make is a trip they don't make across sixty feet of parking garage, and that comes straight off your clock. Does that make sense?' That would have answered his concern with a lever he controls instead of an apology for the estimate.
phone_presence_notes: Real, unforced warmth and local knowledge that the customer responded to — 'Oh! Look at you. Look at that up. Great! I love it' when he turned out to be on the first floor, 'Yes cause I always see Amazon trucks parked right there' about his own property, and a reassurance that landed as genuine partnership ('We're gonna work this out though. We're gonna get you Bobby... I got you covered') — pulled down from a 5 by his name being used exactly once in twenty-eight minutes and long stretches where her side is a wall of 'Okay. Okay. Okay.'
